The putt

Click anywhere on the green to solve a putt from there.

What is being solved

Two nested searches. First the pace: the launch speed that would leave the ball 40 cm past the hole if it did not drop. Then the line: the direction whose closest approach passes through the cup at that pace.

The window is then found by holding that pace and walking the aim outward until the putt stops dropping. The putt you place is solved here, in the page, by the same code as the offline pipeline; the surface layers were solved the same way ahead of time, every pin, every third cell.

Reading the lines

The holing line is coloured by ball speed, fast to slow. The window edges are the extreme aims that still drop, everything between them holes.

The firm and soft lines are the same aim struck harder and softer by the pace miss you pick. Ten per cent is the median error of a tour player, measured over 162,331 tracked putts; twenty is about the 88th percentile. On a green with runoff these are the interesting lines: they are what turns a missed putt into a three-putt.

What the two models are

P(1 putt) is the geometry model: distance and capture window together as a surface, plus aim, cross slope, net rise, entry speed and path length. P(3+ putts) is distance plus what a 5% pace error leaves, and almost all of that is the soft miss. Leaving yourself short predicts three-putting; running past does not. Green, pin, event and player effects are excluded: they cannot transfer to a position nobody putted from, so what is drawn is the tour population, not a player.

Expected putts combines them. Where the solver finds no line that holes it, asked at 35 cm, the scale this surface is resolved to, not at a point, the outcome is composed instead: lay the ball up as near the hole as the slope allows, then hole out from there. P(1 putt) is 0, and the rest follows from the second putt.

What it does not know

This is physics on a surveyed surface, and the probabilities over it are a tour-wide average, not a read on any one player. Green speed is fixed at the value measured for that green that week, from tracked putt decelerations.

Mesh resolution is about 35 cm, so anything finer than that, a spike mark, a fresh pitch mark, grain, is not in here.

Two things to read with care. The surface is drawn everywhere, including further from the pin than any real putt: beyond 25 m this is predicting past 99.87% of the data it was fitted on, and where two holes share a green the far side is included even though a player could not stand there. And the no-line region reads pessimistically, players hole about 5% of those putts and three-putt about 23% of them, against the composition's ~56%, because the mesh stops at the green's edge and a real player can putt out onto the fringe.
